utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom, and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And, Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Roberts, I'd like to remind that you the -- that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, I'm going to ask you some questions about the events in Grubori this morning. As you told the Court, you went there on the 25th of August, 1995 not specifically for the purpose of going to Grubori but to another location within the Plavno valley as part of an UN mission, and that mission concerned the registration of the local inhabitants. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of the purpose of the visit. It was generally the day before that expressed to party of the UN where I was also present issues of security concern. They had shown us the location of a person or maybe two, but I remember the grave of one man who they claim had been shot by Croatian soldiers but the purpose was to discuss security issues in general, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us whether the whether the registration of those people actually took place that morning on the 25th at the school hall where the rendezvous was arranged?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting was not to arrange the registration then. It was to try to facilitate a meeting from the Croatian civilian police from Knin to come and meet with them so that the police rather than the UN whose responsibility it really is is to hear the concerns and requests from the villagers. There was -- at the point of establishing that the Croatian civilian police, although we had been to see them in the police station the evening before after the first meeting on the first -- on the day before, had not arrived. We continued to try and have a general briefing. The reason was that word had got around to other hamlets in Grubori of such a meeting where the Croatian police would be present with the UN and the number of other hamlets represented by villagers who came to that meeting across the valley from Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that meeting it was also arranged that Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Knin, was also going to be with Mr. Romanic and address the local population. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that later, but at the time of going to Plavno that morning, I myself didn't know that was part of the plan or purpose of the Croatian CIVPOL to come with the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you know if there had been a definite time for this meeting that was arranged with Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall, sir, that when we went from the meeting in Plavno at that village the day before it was it was late afternoon when we went to the CIVPOL station in Knin. My colleague Maria Teresa Mauro was there, I think EJ Flynn also, three or four people. I was just standing in the lobby as they discussed with the Croatian police in the police station in Knin the concerns the villagers and the need, if possible, to come to a meeting the next day at about late morning on the 25th, and it was okay, noted, right, from my observation. And we left thinking, okay, that they understood and maybe they will, maybe won't, that we've told them and they've said that they would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 25th of August, was that a day when the weather was bad in that region?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe it when we set off that morning to Plavno from Knin it was cloudy, it was not raining in any extent. During the course of the meeting with the villagers, at the village we had gone to discuss with, there was light drizzle during the course of that hour or so, which later on, in the course of the events around Grubori, was very heavy rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. At some stage, as you've told us, an alert was sounded and it was noticed that there was smoke in Grubori and the upshot was you went in the direction of that hamlet.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't won't to go into great detail on this. We've got your evidence on it and what I'm doing is taking you in staging points to deal with the substance of it. We've no need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You go there with a number of UN people.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is your first visit to that hamlet on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my first visit to Grubori on that morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Had you ever been to the hamlet before?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Grubori, no, I hadn't. I had been to Plavno valley before, but not to Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Is it right that it is remote and inaccessible?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's remote but it is not inaccessible, sir. It's on the steep other side of the valley. You drive around from the main access road leading back to Knin, around to your right pass Besici and up. It's a fair climb, it is narrow, but I wouldn't say it was difficult to get to or to really find. The villagers themselves would know, as they told us and showed us, different routes down to the valley. So I wouldn't say it was hard to find in that sense, but I understand the purpose of your question, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. You needed someone to show you where it was.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jovan Grubor one of the inhabitants of Grubori, had come across to the meeting at the side of the valley and he was in the car at the head showing EJ Flynn and the UN TV crew exactly where it was and we were in about three or four cars, UN cars in that convoy with the various people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's right, is it not, you cannot see the hamlet from the main road?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you cannot, if you are at the main junction to Knin looking up you would see trees and would you not see the rooftops of Grubori, no, you would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know how well you know the area around that. You can see a settlement called Opacici?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Other little settlements but this is particularly secluded from the main road?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the main road, yes, you would you have to head off up and away from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- visible point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you get there on this first visit you do not discover that anyone has been killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would refer -- I'll comment now but refer to my statement in detail, my report 29th August on the whole affair. But when we got there there were three women villagers, they were in a state of panic. They told us that they could not find certain people. We had been told by other people at the foot of the road going up to Grubori who we later discovered were from the village, soldiers came, soldiers came. Buildings were on fire and we ran around to try to see if we could find anybody else alive or needed help. In the rain the UN TV crew took shots and so on. But the only location I think we were taken to, which is immediately at the entrance to Grubori, was the house of Marija Grubor who was 90, and one of the villagers told her that they thought in that still burning ashes was her body, but that was it. We didn't see anything. We decided then the most important thing was to go and report this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your party went back to Knin and a report was made to General Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a report was made to the police station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with Maria Teresa Mauro and EJ Flynn at the meeting we had with Major Colonel Dondo, forgive me, the liaison officer or one of them to General Cermak. I did not go and I'm not completely sure whether exactly at that moment my colleagues went to the CIVPOL station to report it. I myself after the meeting in the lobby or the entrance room of the office of General Cermak went back myself to the headquarters of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've described the three of you. Was there also someone from UNCIVPOL as part of the group?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall there was in that meeting there was -- with interpreter, with a meeting with Colonel Major Dondo, at least three or four people with the interpreter as well. That's the best of my memory, yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were aware at that time, it was the normal procedure for matters to be reported to the local police?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. I think our concurrence, sir, on what we had been seeing, just to digress a very quick moment, in the days and weeks before of hearing these shots from the village of the side, of seeing the smoke, going with Jovan in the car, being shown and seeing what we found directly in front of us, the most apparent thing for me being there was this was something that had happened very, very recently, and we wanted to go directly to establish, first of all, a sort of clear sense of urgency at the office of General Cermak, that something should be done. But you're right, CIVPOL are the -- Croatians are the main body for that. But my colleagues did say to Major Dondo that we wanted to see an investigation which we really felt to be pushed at the level of General Cermak based on past descriptions and that something should be done in terms of security which might be beyond police that he may have the capacity and resources to do. And then I myself left, went back to the Sector South headquarters, and filed a report to my press office in Zagreb briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The purpose of going to General Cermak was because he was there to help the UN with problems and this was seen as an UN problem that he might be able to help with.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that our feeling was that we, my colleagues especially, should leave this at the doorstep of General Cermak based upon our reporting and observations passed to him by my colleagues of a sense of unlawness developing and that he had told us early on at the meeting I referred to yesterday that he was the person who could address these issues. It was a little bit wider than that, I think, just in terms of he could help the UN. We went there to make a distinction. It was a very serious development. We wanted him to be aware of it and to carry out an investigation, urgently. It was happening at that moment. The time to do things was to act, and I am not sure here whether my CIVPOL colleagues in the UN went to the Croatian CIVPOL station to file a report. I understood - careful word, understood - that they had, but we wanted to see action on something that had taken place at the very moment, in Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation to ... The report to the police was something that you don't know whether that took place or not on the 25th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, no. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any coordination between the UN team as to who was doing what and who was reporting to whom?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood later that evening after we had been to Grubori a second time on talking briefly at the UN CIVPOL station that this had been passed to Croatian CIVPOL. I was told that. Beyond that, I thought, okay, well, they've been informed and from a press office point of view, if I'm asked, I can say that the UN have checked with the Croatian police and they have been informed of it. So if not [indiscernible], I would assume that we were informed of it latest on the evening of the day that we had seen what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's no reason to doubt that information, that they were reported it on the 25th to the police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. When Dondo was spoken to, the report there was that there was burning and there was trouble, but he was not informed that there had been any killings.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first refer you to my report again 29th of August, 1995 on this and on the actual description I gave there on the encounter and description of my colleagues and myself to Mr. Dondo. It was made very clear that we had heard shots from across the valley while we were across the valley, a sense of insecurity prevailed from our point of view in Plavno, based upon previous visits before those two days. That the women had told us at the bottom of the road, "soldiers, soldiers," crying and in panic. When we got to the top of the road entering Grubori clearly something very dramatic and violent had happened. Building were burning and I think we emotionally extolled to him this was a situation ongoing, it could get worse, now we need to have action. We did not however say we've seen bodies, there's people discovered by the UN, numbers, no, we did not. It was very forceful, very emotional, that we wanted to see some action take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate then, firstly, that General Cermak only had a unit of nine people under him?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know then that he had what you're saying now is such a limited amount of staff that he, from what you're saying, could personally muster to go and solve problems or help the UN. My understanding, digressing, but I think it's relevant is from what I understood him to say at the meeting on 8th of August and through my colleagues in other meetings since that time, he was the person who had authority to make things happen. I do not see why if we had thought that General Cermak, in all fairness, had such limited resources we would not have then gone directly to his office. We would have gone, I'm sure, through Maria Teresa Mauro, EJ Flynn, not just myself, to the police, to people who we felt had better resources to do things and move things. I think there is a very important distinction, with all respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. That is why I'm putting it to you. You didn't appreciate that he actually didn't have any command over any troops there.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't appreciate that. I'm hearing that now. Again, my understanding from the situation on the time of what was described to us and I heard was that General Cermak portrayed the impression of being a person who had overall authority, and that was the impression that was not just with me but with people like the sector commander, the head of civil affairs and so on who had meetings with him to try and get things addressed in regard to such authority existing. If we were all wrong, well, we should have been advised, I think, of the real terms of reference on paper, but we did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate, for instance, that Dondo wasn't under his command, he was under a completely different line of the Croatian army as a liaison officer? He had a different commander, a Brigadier Plestina?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on seeing him, Colonel Dondo, I also, not at that time but on one or two meetings in the office of General Cermak, was wondering what exactly was the overall remit of the entire structure of the office of General Cermak. It wasn't as far as I understand a regular kind of functioning in the Republic of Croatia to have a garrison commander in such exceptional circumstances after the fall of the Krajina. So, obviously, with perhaps piecemeal with various people doing various things who may have allegiances to other different commander units. I accept that. But my clear impression, sir, is that the expressions given to my colleagues that I heard from General Cermak were to imply that he was a person with authority who could coordinate and guide things, and that's my recollection still. I'm hearing what you've said now for the first time, accept very much sincerely what you've said but I just wonder so much about how things might have been different in many respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If he had power.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If we had, as the UN been clearly aware that General Cermak did not have such authority and did not have the ability to coordinate and to exercise power as I felt, I understood he portrayed that he did. To have on paper your guidelines and terms of reference in a job is one thing. If you say, Well, I will do my best to address that; yes, this is shocking, we must do more to correct this, I will get on to it, I will bring an extra detachment of police to Knin from wherever in Croatia to address these unlawful acts. One thing is okay, if you're saying that, then you have some authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't appreciate that he was saying that because he was trying to help you. That was his whole purpose of being there, was that he was helping you.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's why his door was always open?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can extend that sympathy that I felt many things that General Cermak said to my colleagues, not many of them I heard directly, that he was, I think, very frustrated with a range of issues, but if I in coming to this testimony, look through with all due respect the records of the letters of General Forand, the protest letters, there are 11 of them, submitted by the Sector South commander to General Cermak, four them in a row between late August and 1st September, all protesting the issue of freedom of movement. Why is the chief military officer of the UN doing that? Because I assume, and it is speculation, with due respect that he feels that his counterpart of authority in Knin is General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from General Forand, and I won't go into that and he has spoken for himself on -- on these issues.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, I'm sorry, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Turning back, then, to the 25th, and you go back for a second visit to Grubori by which time it is right that the weather has worsened. Is that a fair description?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I -- I wouldn't agree with you. I -- I can recall very well that it was heavy rain on the time that we left the village across the valley from which we saw these plumes of smoke breaking out. We got up towards Grubori, it was raining quite hard. When we went back in the late afternoon, early evening of the 25th there was some I would say light rain, overcast, but I know when we were in Grubori it was quite light weather with sunshine. And there was not bad weather, no. No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's on this visit that two bodies are discovered, that there has been two recent murders. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on that visit that when we arrived, I think Milica Grubor was taking us and what was the Dutch TV crew that had come with us who had arrived in my office, they went back with us, UN TV did not, and we went to this very narrow doorway about 20 metres away from the entrance of the village, climbed these stairs and there was the body of an elderly man lying by the bed covered in blood around his head. We looked at the scene, there was a CIVPOL officer, as I recall there, and I took four or five shots of that from different angles and I've stated in my report my assessment of how he was shot at close range. I observed cartridges on the floor which I also photographed. The window of the small bedroom was closed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I stop you. Time is limited and it is it not out of any disrespect at all, Mr. Roberts. And it's a shocking scene; let me make that clear. I'm actually interested in these little facts I'm putting to you and how matters develop because there's no issue that the murders happened.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two bodies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Two bodies. And why I put it as starkly as that is that having discovered those two bodies, you then return to Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We photographed quite extensively the two bodies and where the other body of -- I think the elderly man who had his throat slashed in the field where Jovo found him and we photographed, I think my colleagues at the time had found the body of another male in the field with a woman and I recall those were photographed at the same time. So we had, if I'm not wrong - and I have to refer to my report of 29th of August - four bodies and the report of a women saying that her husband was almost for sure in the house that had collapsed from fire. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you saying that you discovered five bodies or four bodies on that second visit on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that had seen the body upstairs, the body in the hallway, there were two bodies in the field, that I know CIVPOL saw. Photographs were taken and we also had this discussion with the wife of a gentleman who was apparently invalid who didn't make it. We never saw the body. She assumed he die in the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because in the UN TV interview the next day at 11.00, only two bodies are mentioned, no more.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It says that, but we had found late afternoon in the team assessment four people, I'm almost sure, at that second visit and I think maybe two days later I photographed again the doorway of Marija Grubor's house and photographed what had we thought was the remains of her arm. This is the 90-year-old lady. And one paragraph in my report explains the sequence of events of -- of finding bodies and photographs, I think, pretty well. When we left that time, we knew for sure we had seen more than two bodies. We had accounted for more or less all of the villagers who were missing in regard to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You returned from there to Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you arrive in Knin after this second visit on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th, well, it was sometime mid-evening around 8.00 or 9.00. I can't put a precise time. It was getting dusky dark for sure. We had been in Grubori the second time, longer than the first occasion in the morning, we had made a pretty thorough assessment the second time, and Jovo and Milka had showed us what they had discovered in the afternoon while we were not in there, so it was about an hour, hour and a half, maybe we were in Grubori and then went back to Knin, which took about 45 minutes, went back to the headquarters of Sector South myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't file a fresh report at the police station in relation to the number of bodies.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if that happened, sir. I went myself directly to the HQ Sector South. I don't know whether my colleagues did or did not. When I returned that evening, my colleagues filed quite broader reports on what had happened, EJ Flynn, especially, I think. I began preparing something I did not complete that night and I popped in to the UN CIVPOL office to ask, okay, you know what has happened, has it been passed on, and that's what I was referring to before, they said yes, the police had been informed and so on. I did not add to that what I had seen or observed in the second visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't go back to Dondo and say to him in fact we have now discovered four murders --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yeah, that's correct. No, I did not. I do not know if my colleagues had a second visit with him. My understanding is that they did not, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you have seen no information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I have seen no report from CIVPOL, from civil affairs saying they had a second meeting that evening, that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So then we move to the 26th, and -- which is the next day, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just look at two documents which have been in evidence or two pages of a document that has been in evidence. It's Exhibit D57. May we turn to page 59. It's box 193 dated the 26th of August, 1995. It's the Knin daily log-book. And the English will be coming soon, box 193. Page 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document that's in evidence, Mr. Roberts, to help you. It's the log-book down at the Knin police station. We see at 3.00 the commander of that police station, Milos Mihic. Did you know Mr. Mihic?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of a working relationship, I knew he was the commander, I observed him several times, at the police station lobby with my colleagues. We didn't have any direct interaction, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He reported that two male bodies were found and we see that Mr. Romanic agreed to do an on-site investigation as written in that box.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see those two --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Two bodies being found.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No report of the four or five bodies at that stage.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it's saying here, yeah. That's what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go back to Grubori on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I recall on the 26th of trying to go to Plavno again, which, if I'm not mistaken was a Sunday, and it was with CIVPOL and human rights -- one of the human rights action team interpreters and I did not put this in my report, but on that afternoon we got to the edge of Plavno and a police check-point blocked us from going into Plavno, and my recollection is that it was the next day, the 27th, that a group of us had returned again to talk to the people who were still there, because earlier, on the -- on the day we left on the 25th, I think there was some concern of their security but they had said for now, although in shock and distressed, that they were okay to stay where they were. That was 25th, and now on the 26th, I recall we did not get to Grubori or Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll turn now to page 61 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would it be of any use to explore about any issue of the 26th being a Sunday or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If I neglected to say it, I meant to say it in my own mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Roberts, 26th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was a Saturday. 27th is a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 26th is a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say your recollection is that it was a Sunday. Could there be any confusion about the chronology, because according to my information the 26th was a Saturday, not a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt that we went back again the day after, sir, so it would have been a Saturday, if the 26th was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Sundays didn't have a different rhythm from Saturdays or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So there could be no confusion that you rather -- that your recollection is rather that you went back on Sunday rather than the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt almost for sure we went back again because of the seriousness of it and it was a CIVPOL team and we didn't get to Plavno on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 61, we're looking here at box 197 and 26th of August, 1995 at 2000. And you see the name Dondo there, Karolj Dondo.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there's the report there of five bodies. Do you see --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see in the event --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And that's at 8.00. Were you aware of Mr. Dondo visiting Grubori on that day of the 26th, in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly if I knew that Mr. Dondo was there. I know that there was a visit quite quickly after by General Cermak, who went to the village and was accompanied by a number of Croatian press and made a statement from the village describing what he said had taken place, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was on the 27th. That was on the 27th. Let's turn to -- just looking at those pieces of information there, they're compass points, let's turn to the UN TV report, which we know took place on the 26th of August at about 11.00 in the morning, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P504.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is now the 26th. And is it right that, in fact, this was an unscheduled visit to Mr. Cermak's office that morning by UN TV and one of its purposes was to ask him questions about Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for this to come up. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm giving you the generality. No need to look at the specific, just answer -- I do that to save Court time.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I am aware that they had sought an interview with General Cermak personally, were granted one and went to make that interview for UN TV, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you present at that interview?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present during the interview, no, with the UN TV crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you knew it was taking place?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they had requested a meeting through Colonel Dondo or his office, I think both things had happened through the UN TV guys, and they had been granted and went to have the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the B/C/S transcript wasn't on the screen and it is now there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the questions of UN TV to General Cermak, did you consider the questions that were to be asked by the particular interviewer?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall whether we had some discussion about the kinds of questions to ask. I don't think that I had proposed specific questions that should be asked. It was the UN TV crew that, anyway, even if colleagues might make proposals or I, it was for them in the end to decide what to ask, and in those kind of situations it depends on the responses of the interviewee as to how an interview develops regardless of what might be in your mind to ask, but general areas. But I can't recall that I drafted something that they must ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You agree that the report given to Dondo the previous day was that there had been fire trouble but that there had been no report of the murders that you had found, be it two bodies, four bodies, to Dondo or the office of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's a fair description. There was nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, that the wrong document in Croatian is on the screen -- a wrong translation in English is on the screen. It's -- P504 should be 03062714. There have been several versions of this document, Your Honour, in the proceedings as disclosed and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they are apparently all attached to this one, because I have 00572865 which apparently was on the screen, and yes, the other one you just mentioned is also attached. Could the parties sit together and see whether we have one translation attached whereas as a matter of fact it is a -- I don't know to what extent it is a transcript or a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I've got three translations attached to it. Could the parties sit together and find which is the best and then the others would be removed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm told the second is the perfected one and I see nodding from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we could get that one on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is the one I'm working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Roberts, these are matters that have to be attended to for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, apparently we're okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this interview, if we just go through it very quickly and then I'll be finished in all my questioning, we can see the first question, answer, second question, second answer, and General Cermak said: "Yes, I know about these events." And in his answer to the question about whether he knew what had happened in Grubori in the last two days, was about a Serb terrorist being arrested, one body being found, we believe it was the body of a Croatian army soldier, because hands were tide with wire behind the back. No mention there of any Serbian people being killed by him. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The response in the interview was describing what had happened from General Cermak's perspective. I think that is quite clear and talks about the causes of what he says the causes are for the incident in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what he says, two houses were burned, there had been a wounding, an arrest and the body. The first mention of villagers being killed is actually by the UN interviewer. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I think it's further down --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. It's on that page. It is the last question on page 1, were two dead old men, sick in bed in his pyjamas --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- shot in the back of the head?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just draw your attention, sir, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to a couple of points. It's only my personal observation. General Cermak seems to be very well informed of this military special unit sweep team. He gives there the fact that they found 70 civilians of Serbian ethnicity who were taken care of who stayed in their houses. Now, bear in mind this is the same time, the same day that the UN party across the village, across the valley with a good many -- good many civilians for the meeting on the morning, and I've not put it in my report but there were more than 20 villagers at that meeting put on the record now approximately that number, and then he talked further down the kind of combat activity, combat that took place in this village, questioned to himself. Generally a mopping up operation and achieving encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then when I saw this by my colleagues in transcribing of the tape I asked, Do you know seriously that General Cermak said some 500 to 700 members of the special police or do you think you're mistaken and it was 50 to 70 and they said no, it is 500 to 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So quality of information?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just thinking when I saw that and asked them and they said, no, he did say 500 to 700, I was a bit astonished because, why? The number of hamlets there are around Plavno, yes, it is a bit of speculation again, but just the isolation of the place and how many possible Serb bandits, if you like, are on the run there. It suggests a large operation is my only overall assessment on reading that, a large operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I take your observation and we've got the point, so what I'll put to you is this. If he's wrong about that, his information is wrong, he doesn't know what he's talking about. Would you agree? If he's wrong about that? Do you see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that he seems very assured at saying 500 to 700 people as if he does know that that was the number or the number he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've had evidence in court about the number.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right. So if he is wrong about that, you agree his information is bad. He doesn't know what he is talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you're asking for kind of conclusions which are pretty useless, if you say, A where the truth is B, then either you are not informed about B and therefore you say A, it could also be that you'll well-informed about B but for whatever reason you say A. So, therefore, asking this kind of conclusions from a witness doesn't assist the Chamber because it doesn't resolve the -- what may be the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I allowed the witness free reign, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the witness couldn't answer the question unless he has specific knowledge and then he should be specifically asked about it whether he had any reasons why A was said rather than what some people say that B was the correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, he said he didn't know that people were killed in Grubori. If we go to page 2 of the document, we see in the second answer: "Again, I don't know where the gentleman has this information from about two civilians killed." The next answer: "I don't know. I'll find out. I don't know if this morning there was anybody with the people up there." That's what he was saying, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He didn't know?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I read the transcript, having been in Grubori, and, yes, you're right, we did not report to Mr. Dondo the number of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any bodies.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's -- let's --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not respond about any bodies being seen or found at that time when we went to report to Mr. Dondo. I had the impression that at the beginning General Cermak is stating what has happened, that he is aware of this incident, and then later, when it is put to him clearly by the UN TV crew who he does not know had been there and filmed is a kind of different reaction, saying, I don't know where you got this information, well, the UN TV, sir, had been there, had filmed it, and they had seen by that time the tape of the Dutch TV crew because my understanding is they swapped tapes and they clearly had good visual information in terms of what happened in terms of the fire and the bodies being discovered, which at this time it seems that General Cermak does not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And at the top of that page -- at the top of that page, in the first question, the interviewer says: "...the Croatian police went to the local larger village but they haven't yet been to the village where the burning took place?" Are you able to shed any light on that, bearing in mind this interview was 11.00 in the morning of the 26th and the statement there by the interviewer that the police had been there? Are you able to help with that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reading the paragraph. Just one second. I can't shed any light in terms of the UN TV crew interviewer knowing for sure unless that information from CIVPOL, but I don't know that the Croatian police had been to the larger village in the way that the question is suggesting that he had firm information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, in the second question on that page, they say they were there that morning.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he says: "There's been no Croatian police presence in that village." We take that to mean Grubori.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the answer here of where it says: "General, I don't wish to contradict. We were there this morning --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- and there has been no Croatian police presence in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We take that to mean Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Meaning the Croatian police have not been to commence any kind of investigation within the period by which this interview took place is the claim of the colleagues of UN TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seemed they had been at the local larger village, as the first question indicates?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear, though, do you agree that where that local larger village is, it could be at the bottom of the valley at Besici. It could be another hamlet in Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As we've seen, in fact, the first report is after this interview of two bodies to the Croatian police that we have recorded in the Knin police log-book. After this interview.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's later on that that's recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you, in fact, as part of this UN team, not focussed clearly on how to deal with this incident properly, that you didn't follow it up properly?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure we could not have done more in covering all the bases, perhaps. I can't speak for my colleagues who would have that kind of decision making process, not me as the press officer. I don't know this exact specifics of it, only to the extent of a meeting with Mr. Dondo and clear expression, as we've said, of wanting to see urgent reaction and at the time it was said to him, Please ensure that General Cermak is fully informed of this because we want to see him that afternoon. And he wasn't there, which is why we informed Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you, for instance, on that day, the 26th, as the questioner said, would Mr. Cermak go up to Grubori with them? Did anyone go to his office later that afternoon and say, We will take you there?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. You know -- you have never seen a report to that at all?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen that at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. But we do know that his men went up there later that day.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later that day, then you'll concur is the 26th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that then is more than 24 hours after General Cermak's office has been informed on the late morning of the 25th of a very disturbing violent incident where gunshots are heard and scenes of distress are recorded by the UN and asking for urgent action and an investigation report was made very clear and we were told that we passed on to General Cermak, and that was the morning of the 25th. So that's over a day later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No deaths were reported till this interview at 11.00 --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to him?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I understand what you're saying. I'm afraid, sir, that an incident at a hamlet where we have seen civilians in distress and we have heard gunshots is for me a clear issue to address that the civilian police be sent there or those under whose authority it is be sent to ensure security and commence an investigation, first of all at least, of arson, first of all, at least of distress and destruction, which were clearly made apparent to Mr. Dondo, and we're now looking at issues which are over one whole day later and we're talking about a distance that can be covered in less than 45 minutes driving time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that Dondo had no command over the police? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know he had no authority. Again, I am finding myself now back in the days almost of Knin, sir, which is that the UN must go to the police and report what we've seen and basically escort them to a place where we've seen distressing scenes. We reported this to what we understood was, as I said before and repeating myself now, the senior authority official in Knin, and I do not say we did everything right. No, I would not say that. I can say myself I thought there was some gaps. But is it not for the office of General Cermak to go to, to make a phone call? They have more kind of authority and persuasion on the police, I think, than we do, from several experiences of passing on incidents to the Croatian police previous to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts and Mr. Kay, as well in putting questions to the witness, what should have been done and what could have been done are questions of a mixed nature. It comprises both factual elements but also whether or not priorities should have been given and what the number of people were available, what else there was to be done. I think that the matter has been covered in a way which gives hardly any expectation that we come any further. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that General Cermak had no right or ability to investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that he had no authority to investigate crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Next in line, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, let me just get set up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile I can inform Mr. Roberts that the next one who will cross-examine you is Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Kay, the Chamber notes that where you indicated that you needed two hours yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably less, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kuzmanovic, I was addressing Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Almost two hours, but I do see that for you to ask is also 65 minutes. That's appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, I'd like to follow up a little bit on a discussion you had with Mr. Kay. The list that you put together of the vehicles at the scene, it's P692.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If that can be called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a notation on the right, it says AR. I'm assuming that is Alun Roberts, correct, handwritten?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very top right. Yes, that's my initial, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 1-2008, I'm assuming that's January 2008 or if you can explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the date that it was, I think submitted or handed in to -- it's like sort of a mark of identity with the investigation part of the Tribunal, I think. It wasn't on there at the time the note was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had testified yesterday, I believe, that you thought the note was written on the 25th of August of 1995. But this is the second list that you had written, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What the sequence of this is, I -- I had written --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, I understand you want to explain. My question to you was this is the second list you had written, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the second list, yes, on leaving the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The first list you said had 10 to 12 vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the list you couldn't find?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the list we couldn't find.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you put together a second list of -- where six vehicles are noted and a white vehicle with no plates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on leaving the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And these are registration plates for these vehicles. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not give this document to the Croatian police at any time, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a pretty important piece of potential evidence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I shared this with colleagues from CIVPOL and with UNHCR who I also thought took a list as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the first time this list of vehicles shows up anywhere in any report is in Elisabeth Rehn's report of November 1995, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware it appeared for the first time in her report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not give this list of vehicles to the Croatian police with registration numbers for vehicles at or near the scene of where the alleged crime occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I passed this to CIVPOL and I felt this had been passed on. I also shared it with UNHCR and I understood also that the UNHCR had taken a similar list, a longer list, a full list of the 11 vehicles concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see in the police log-book -- Mr. Kay showed you the police log-book. There was no list of vehicles contained in the police log-book. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You took photographs at the scene yourself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you provide those photographs to the Croatian civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem with some of the photographs taken in around Knin was the issue of developing them, of being safe and many of those photographs were not developed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was not my question, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they are theoretically and most certainly what happened in Plavno was essentially a crime scene, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the distinct impression that myself and my colleagues had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And photographs that you took at that crime scene potentially could benefit a police investigation, could it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could, and I think also one was on the receiving end wondering what the Croatian civilian police might have done as well with the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask for the benefit of interpretation and the transcript to make a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, strike two. I will slow down. I get six strikes here, though, right, Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The photographs taken at the scene, I think you said were not provided to the Croatian civilian police but you essentially were the first people on the scene. Correct? Meaning the UN.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pausing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were the first people on the scene of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you were not a forensic expert, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You are not a crime scene investigator?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You are not a coroner?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously these people were tragically killed in this village, but as far as a specific cause of death from a forensic standpoint, you could not tell us that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a photograph that you took of Mr. -- I think his name was Jovan Grubor showing someone -- the particular area where one civilian -- the area in which he had been killed outside, correct? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jovo showed us the place where he had been killed or said he had been -- he found them dead at, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's P693. Before we get to that document I wanted to ask you a few more questions, sir, about P692. At the bottom of this page, there is it some handwritten note regarding Rade in Bijeljina. What was the purpose of writing -- can you explain that significance, please?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it bears no relation to the information -- if you just scroll up. Yes, I think this is information back in Knin headquarters that I just had the paper and scribbled on a phone number which was of no relation to the actual information on the note pad. It may have been that it was covered by some other paper and went through, but I think it was on that same piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Ika Todorovic at the bottom here at UNHCR Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a contact office of the UNHCR in Belgrade and a phone number alongside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please explain the purpose of -- if any, of that notation regarding UNHCR Belgrade on this document?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is completely unrelated on irrelevant to what happened on what is on that piece of paper. It is just a by-chance add, addition of some information of Bijeljina, a phone number, and Ika Todorovic, phone number in Belgrade. It is not related at all to any of the information above that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any -- what contact, if any, did you have with Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any direct contact with him on this matter. I think UNHCR from Knin may have done. In regard to some of the people who later went to Belgrade in the big bus convoy, I know only there was contact between Benny Otim, the UNHCR chief in Knin, with Mr. Todorovic, who was the I think legal affairs office at UNHCR in Belgrade, but I was not in contact with Mr. Todorovic on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, I note that during the course of the disclosure of evidence -- or documents over the past few weeks relating to you, there are many documents we hadn't seen before, this P692 being one of them. Do you happen to have your own trove of archived documents in your office?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have many documents we kept from the UN public affairs office in Knin, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you disclose all of the documents related to events surrounding this particular case to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all of the documents that I made or produced as reports on this issue have all been handed over and I have also handed over to the investigators each of the respective sitreps reports of UNMOs, UNCIVPOL and Human Rights Action Teams that corroborates the information of my I think 12th of October report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So those are all documents that you kept copies of and you have in your personal possession?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are there any documents in your possession related to this matter that have you not produced to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this matter of Grubori or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On this case in general, relating to this case, Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have kept in my possession, I think, most of the reports of the various UN departments operating in Sector South since I arrived there in 1993, not every single document but a good section of the work of UNCIVPOL, UNMOs, UN humanitarian affairs, et cetera as kind of a record, historic record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, I think the question was whether you had any documents which you had not produced to the Office of the Prosecutor, not what you actually had in your possession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have given everything that I think is useful to this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Roberts, in relation to P692 whether at any point in time you know of anyone that gave this specific list of vehicle plates to any Croatian police office?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this list, I don't know anyone who gave this list to any Croatian official authorities, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The archive of your own personal documents that you have, where is that located?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of it is in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And where is the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of it is in Banja Luka at the former UN office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there still an UN office in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some of it is in my apartment. A lot of it is in New York and in my private accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where is your apartment located?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my apartments is in -- is located in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reside in two locations, New York and in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you currently do for a living, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the present time I am not actually working. I completed a contract with the international court in The Hague and I have doing some private work, consulting work both in relation to international organisations and NGO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say international court in The Hague, you're not talking about the ICTY, are you?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the ICC?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P693, if that could be pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, is that Mr. Grubor standing on the left with the cane?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the gentleman on the right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN CIVPOL. I don't know his actual name, but I think the investigators have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the location at which you testified that Mr. Grubor found one of his neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this is a location that Jovo took us to after he had showed us the body of the gentleman in the front lobby with throat slashed. He said he had not found him there and took us to a nearby field not very far away where he showed where the body was found, and this the photograph of him pointing to where he said he found the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular spot, and I don't doubt for a moment that the gentleman that you saw in the room was the same gentleman, but there is no evidence of any kind to show that there was a body there, blood, or anything, is there?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just -- the photograph shows what it shows and that's all I've said in the caption, that he showed us the location where he said he found the body he took or dragged to the front lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that Mr. Grubor here on the left dragged the body of the dead gentleman back into a house?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said. I understood he had some help to drag him. That's his description, that he pulled him back into the lobby, the reason why was -- why did you do that, was that okay, in terms of pigs or animals or problems, he put him back inside the -- the front lobby of his own apartment, which was partly burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. How long of a distance was it from this particular spot to where the gentleman's body was?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not so very far, maybe, hmm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You said 250 metres in the statement, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that I said that. It was a closer distance to the field from the actual front of the apartment. It was not big a distance away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone had done anything to that particular body like change its clothes or clean it up or anything like that before you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean inside the lobby of the apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of somebody come to do what you have stated. We're talking, I think, about four or five hours between when the UN was there in the morning and when we went back in the late afternoon, evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So that is the same day that you came back and this is the position at which Mr. Grubor found the dead body, and from this position in the photograph, 693, the body was dragged some distance, considerable or not, into a house. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he described, yes. We saw the body lying in the lobby of the house which is where the photographs were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This photograph obviously was not taken in the house, right? You're referring to other photographs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. This photograph is outside in the field as I have described. This is it where he said that body was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any shell casings that were found at or about this position?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I did not go and really look. I don't think I took many photographs, maybe even just one or two of this particular scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you note any in this area evidence of people who had been traversing through the area? It was raining, was it not? People would leave tracks with boots. It was muddy. Did you see any of that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. It was a field -- the front here on the photographs was a field with grass. I did not see signs of lots of people or lots of boots or whatever in regard to what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the way to get to this particular hamlet of Grubori, you had described briefly during your examination by Mr. Kay. This was not a paved road that led to Grubori, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way you got there, no sir. You would go to Besici on a tarmac road, turn left and swing up and then you begin climbing a gravel, mud road going up, which is basically one track vehicle more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So for one to get to Grubori, especially in the weather the way it was on the day that you were there, you would pretty much need either a beast of burden or a four-wheel drive vehicle. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly suitable for UN-type vehicles which had four-wheel drive to go up there, yeah. They were all UN jeeps, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That of course was not the question. The question was focussing on whether you needed that to go there. That you could easily -- or reach it if you had a four-wheel drive is of course different from whether you couldn't get there without a four-wheel drive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to -- thank you, Your Honour. On that context you could easily walk to the village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But from the question it is clear that Mr. Kuzmanovic is interested to know that if you wanted to drive there, whether you would -- then he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you would need a four-wheel drive vehicle but certainly something that we would use was very easy to get there, UN vehicles, four-wheel drive, pick-up, something quite strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're not certain about whether you would make it if you had a non-four-wheel drive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or an old kind of vehicle, I think it would be difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, the road itself was a basically a one-lane road, correct, I mean, if there was someone else coming the opposite way, there was no way for the vehicles to pass?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please pull the map up that you had drawn. And I will find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's P694, if I'm not mistaken. Your Honour, it might be a good time for a break, since I can't find the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the best reasons I have heard for a break. We will have a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you may continue with making pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, we'd left off -- before we get to the map that I have found, the map that you drew, I wanted to get back to the issue of Mr. Grubor and the photograph that you took. If we could go to P677, please. That's your statement dated February of 2007. And if we could go to page 11.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment I'm seeing the map or the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The efficient registrar was ready with my map, so I changed gears on her. The second paragraph of this statement, Mr. Roberts, this is when you went back to Grubori on the first day. If you looked in the middle of the paragraph toward the right it says: "The elderly man of the village," and I'm assuming Mr. Grubor, correct, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the top paragraph now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The second paragraph which, which --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "The elderly man of the village," and that is Mr. Grubor, correct, the man whom you've photographed?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Took us to a field where we found the body of a male person who had been killed with his throat cut." Now according to statement, I will continue with the statement, the body of this man was taken to the hallway of a house, and I took photographs of him there. Now, Mr. Roberts, your statement in 2007, a little more than a year and a half ago, tells us that you were at the spot where the body was found and then moved and that you observed the body taken to the hallway.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. As I've said in my statement yesterday, this statement is 2007. I stand by my statement that describes this in quite some detail of 1997 and my report of 12th October. This is the wrong way around and it's -- I apologise, it's the wrong interpretation. We photographed the body, first of all, in the hallway, as is accurately recorded in those reports, I think, and we were shown the body first of all by Jovo in the lobby of the house which he said was the house of the subject who had been killed and we saw him then and photographed him with his throat cut in the lobby, as the photograph I think display. Later he took us to show us the location where he said the body of this man was found by him killed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Roberts, you gave what, six statements or so throughout the course of this investigation, and in this particular statement there is no proofing note or supplementary statement correcting that this was in error, is there, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no correction to this particular reference to this 2007 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about this issue of the throat being cut. Now, you said before you're not forensic expert, you're not a criminal investigator, but it would be pretty logical, would it not, that if someone's throat is cut, there's going to be quite a bit of blood and that blood is going to be remaining either in the spot where the person was found or the spot where the person was dragged, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you said, I'm not an expert, so I'm not going to comment in terms of what an expert might have found. I will concur that when I went to see the field, I did not in the photograph portray any blood found at the scene. I think if you or we look at the photograph itself, it shows what it shows, the conclusion of us, is this man had a number of stab wounds and his throat had been slashed. I'm not saying any more in terms of how it happened or why that's what the photograph shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 8 of your statement, this same one.
