And if we look at the fifth paragraph from the bottom, it says: "Jovo Grubor who had been brought into a house from the meadow and who appeared to have had his throat cut." Now, in this particular portion of the statement, you said that it appeared to have been cut, not that it was cut.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here. That's what I said, yes, it appeared to have his throat cut. The cause of death appeared to be that his throat was cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Whether that in fact happened or whether it didn't happen, you don't know. That's an accurate statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw what I recorded, that his throat was cut. I can't say that's definitely the cause of death, but we observed this man lying with his throat severed, cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 3 of P679, which is your statement of 4 March 2008. And we go to paragraph 12. And the last sentence of that paragraph says: "I understood that Jovo Grubor had his throat slashed." So that is the third variation of that particular theme. I mean, it's fair to state, Mr. Roberts, that you didn't know whether it's the throat slashed or whether it wasn't slashed or whether it was a bullet that grazed his vein or anything?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think myself, looking at this statement, the one I made in 1997 and the detailed report of 12th October 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not -- Mr. Roberts, that is it not my question. That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't hear any question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the witness may continue his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, the direction you are coming from. I see that the word used here throughout these statements is "throat cut," "throat slashed," and on finding the body and taking the photographs, my opinion as a press officer was he had died a violent death of which the wound most outstanding was the severely slashed throat, his throat was cut --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you as a press officer have no specific medical knowledge to say whether his throat was cut or whether it wasn't cut?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I could see, sir, was a man lying with his throat severely slashed, and that is what the caption says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you manipulate the body to see whether or not -- what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not manipulate the body. What had happened is Jovo had obviously turned over the body from I understand where he placed it face down so that the colleagues and myself, UN colleagues could see the extent of the wound, that he wanted us to see as what he had said was the cause of death and the way he found him, and we photographed from, I think three or four angles the main wound and I think the top of his chest which had another stab wound, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you take his shirt off to determine that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. It is not my job to go start doing things now that you have suggested I have no expertise for. I photographed the body for the record. My colleagues from CIVPOL were there, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any kind of death certificate or forensic report related to that death?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen any forensic report or investigation report of that death or the deaths in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When I had asked you earlier when I showed you the photograph of Mr. Grubor pointing out the spot, you had said initially that he had dragged the body there himself and then after the photograph, you had recalled that he was helped by someone to drag the body to where you ended up photographing it. Who helped him? The two elderly ladies that were in the village?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure. That's the only people who were there, sir, when we went back on the late afternoon and he said that he had dragged him bag to his hallway. And, yes, I can recall we asked, By yourself or alone. He said, Well, Marija, others, which were the two women that were in the village at the same time we went back. This is what he told us he had done to bring the body back inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P690, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the map that you discussed yesterday, Mr. Roberts. The top of this has again your initials AR and then the number slash 2/2008. Is that when you tendered this to the Prosecution as something they could potentially use?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is accompanied with the note of the vehicle tablet numbers. They had been together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So this map and the vehicle tablet numbers were two documents that were made at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes [inaudible], yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us when this particular map was drawn?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map was drawn more or less the day after or within a few days of the actual incident in Grubori, portraying the roads we had been on and the main aspects of that particular visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the original of this is? I know I can see it looks like a colour on -- on the screen and --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. Well, if it got dirty or muddy in terms of papers that it was with, and at the time I don't know what this colouring was. It's not anything for effect. It was just in terms of what it was lying under had collected on the face of the actual piece of note pad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The bottom of this map there's an arrow pointing to Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then there's a squiggly line above, if we can scroll down just little bit.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right above that the arrow there, do you see that squiggly line there?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That is to show the road is kind of broken. That road continues on to Knin is the significance of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So there is some distance between -- of the road between those squiggly lines showing that that's not the exact scale of how far or close it is to Knin. There's some distance in there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what I think is normal in a sketch, you just show that that's the broken road that goes to Knin and this the main portion that comes into the junction of the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously the map is not drawn to scale. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. It's just a sketch map. It's not a map. It is a sketch I think is the proper word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you go up the left side of the road here, is that road paved?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a -- yes. This is at the time -- I don't know how it is now. This was a tarmac road suitable for vehicles. You could certainly, although narrow, have two vehicles passing in either direction on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then -- I'm just waiting for the interpretation. The vehicles that you depict here, a line of 11 blue and white jeeps and mini-bus/vans, which way were they facing?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were facing in the direction that road continues as if they had been, this is also speculation, as if they had been driven in and they were facing in the way we were going to the village we were going to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there's another sort of a squiggly line just above that. Is that also designed to depict that there's some additional road there?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is additional distance up to -- from where the vehicles were toward where we turned left to go to the village that we were meeting the Serb civilian villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the previous answer was rather confusing. Let me see whether I have understood it well. You have in your sketch the vehicles are -- you could consider them to be at the right side of the road or to the left side of the road depending on where they were heading. Now, if I would say that there are situated on the right side of the road seen in the direction they were facing, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they're on the right side of the road facing the direction upwards on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Upwards on the sketch. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So if we're looking at it obviously in the top view, the front of the first vehicle would be where the headlights would be?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is where the cursor is now. They'd be facing -- they are all facing in the same direction on the right in the direction the UN team were going to this visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go back to the junction for a moment and the school and community hall to the right of the junction and that's the place where you -- where you were going to meet?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting was in the village, sir. If you carry on up in the direction past the vehicles on the right where the squiggle is, that road goes on. If you stayed on that road all the way around and did not go left to this hamlet called Zecevici here, you carry on to the top end of the Plavno valley and you can go no further. There are other roads off to the left as you go around. We were there the day before at this same village that I described earlier, to save time for the Court, and we were going to meet the villagers again with the Croatian police at that village to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That village, are you referring to that hamlet or -- because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, that hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That village is where we see several villages. It is it not very clear. So Zecevici hamlet, that is where you would meet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's where -- those are supposed to be houses, sir. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no, no. I do understand that these are houses but -- or other hamlets as well on the sketch. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As you go back to the junction and toward the school, community hall, then you go up again toward the top toward the Grubori hamlet, and before we get to the Grubori hamlet there appears to be a hard right turn that you would have to make. Would the road continue going straight up? Did you just not depict that road there? Was there another road there?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where you go to the -- if you'd move the cursor back to the left where that junction is, there was a small hamlet there and you're climbing. That road to the right was maybe -- if you go to the right with the -- doesn't maybe go hard right like that and then hard left. It was more of a curve upwards towards Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was all a climb?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're climbing up from that point, certainly, yes, and you're climbing up slowly from the direction of the school, community hall. These villages -- these two locations at the bottom of the hamlet is Besici and you go up from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this Grubori --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, from that point here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there, is of course for the record is not very helpful for those. What we've seen that the cursor was moving and apparently the witness agreed with that, from the Zecevici hamlet then on the -- if I could consider the north -- the top of this map to be north, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That facilitates describing. So then to go southerly direction of the map -- of the road we find on the left of the map, up to the junction described, then to go in an easterly direction, passing school, community hall, then turning to the north again, to what appears to be a -- a bend in the road, where the road further up north is not continuing in this sketch, I think the witness said that from there the road was climbing and these were not angles but rather winding, and up -- going up to Grubori. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask the assistance of the usher, if we could get a blue pen for Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you to mark that, Mr. Roberts, in the upper right-hand corner of the drawing is the Grubori hamlet. Is that where the road ends?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The squiggly line before it is -- is representing that the road continues a little bit further up. It was not much but it was a bit longer a climb up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you could just mark for us on this -- on the road itself near the school or -- and community hall or anywhere, which would be responsive to the question where the road starts climbing toward Grubori.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: About here is where it would start climbing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And certainly here steeply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's I think the usual way of indicating that the climb is more -- is steeper to put three arrows in the direction of -- of climbing. Yes, I meant on the line of the road, but apparently this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see on maps if I try to find my holiday locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. It's not very --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's all right. We're not all artists, so don't worry about it. We'll note for the record that where the three squiggly lines are, that's where the climb starts becoming fairly intense and at the bottom of the blue line is where you start climbing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Waespi. Therefore, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit D695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D695 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kuzmanovic, the Chamber, I at least, I will further check on one of the huge military maps we have, but on all the maps that we have at this moment to say that we have a clear picture of exactly where Grubori is, we have it on one map indicated, the map in the series of maps we received from the Prosecution, which gives no details at all. Of course, the Judges are very familiar with Google Earth and these kind of things. At the same time it doesn't give much information, especially about names of hamlets. If there would be a detailed map or if you could produce with sufficient detail, and again I have to check whether it is on the military maps. If it's there, then of course there is no need, but on all other maps we have at this moment, we're a bit lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there was a map tendered through Mr. Janic that has a semi-detailed view of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have the number, then I will immediately check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it off the top of my head, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll find one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and make it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is there, of course there is it no need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will move on to another exhibit, Your Honours, and another area. P691, please, page 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence, it relates -- and I will represent to you, Mr. Roberts, this is your 29 August 1995 Grubori village report by Sector South press office. The last line notes that it was decided to record the licence numbers and for UN TV to film them, and you're talking about the vehicles that were seen in the Plavno valley. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what that relates to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you provide the video to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the video directly. The UN TV had the main video, which was then cut into an edit broadcast version and was shown as part of the UN TV series on various TV channels in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I guess my question is that you -- in answer to my question, you did not provide that to the Croatian police, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether UN TV provided that to Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had thought they certainly gave one to CIVPOL. I cannot say that for sure, but that's as far as I know, I do not think the UN TV crew gave a copy to the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If question go to the next page of that document, please, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 of this report says: "After going on to the Sector South HQ to inform senior Sector South personnel of the attack and filing reports to our offices at mission HQ, we decided to return to Grubori to check on the villagers were safe." And I will stop there. In this particular portion of the report there is nothing that discusses going to report this to the Croatian civilian police, is there?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my report there, there's not. It is describing exactly what you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you went to Sector South, you informed senior Sector South personnel, and those reports that you filled in would go to mission HQ, which presumably is in Zagreb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But nothing was given to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said there I'm recording what I did. I said before in earlier cross-examination that I understood on the return that evening that the Croatian police had been informed by UN CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go -- okay. I'll move on to another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to P684.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, this is a 12 October 1995 memo from the public information office, Sector South, which discusses human rights violations. And if you go, and I will give you the reference to the stamped page numbers on the upper right, to the last four numbers are 8107.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stamped page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You'll see on the upper right -- if the registrar will see on the upper right, there's a number that starts 06348096. And that's how this document is page numbered, because I don't see any page numbers on the document otherwise. You'll see on the upper right-hand corner 0348107.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 of this document discusses UN CIVPOL Knin and that's UN civilian police, not Croatian police, correct, UN CIVPOL, just so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the United Nations civilian police and this is reporting on assessing the joint patrols issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The joint patrols between the Croatian police and UN CIVPOL Knin and it says: "The third time in a row for the Croatian place to cancel the joint patrol with Knin UN CIVPOL team because of lack of vehicles or manpower." Now was it your experience on -- based upon your observations into October of 1995 when this report was issued that the Croatian civilian police had a lack of vehicles and manpower?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going on what my colleagues from CIVPOL informed me and of my own visits not often to the CIVPOL station in Knin, that I would say fair assessment, I didn't see at any one time more than maybe four or five vehicles parked outside the UN CIVPOL station in Knin, and I think speculative, my colleagues in CIVPOL did feel this was clearly a combination of problem and a lack of resources by that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the vehicles normally that you would have for the specifically for UN CIVPOL but even for the Croatian police would be four-wheel drive vehicle, would they not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure. They were the familiar blue jeep vehicles. Some of them we saw in Knin were not exactly new but that's what the -- be the recognised standard Croatian CIVPOL police vehicle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the following paragraph again reports a meeting with the Knin police commander. He is identified as the Knin Croatian policija commander, Zvonko Gambiroza and it says: "In the meeting UN CIVPOL team was informed that joint patrols with Croatian policija are to be cancelled owing to lack of manpower and vehicles in the Croatian police and at the same time commander Gambiroza, said that the Cro-policija recently established some additional check-points in the villages to prevent new criminal actions in the area." Did you in any way observe that these additional check-points were established?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not observe that, no. It's -- for reference, these are the three sources at the bottom describe or corroborate that meeting from CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your experience at least from what you observed, and I think I asked you that to some extent regarding paragraph 11, that there was a lack of manpower and vehicles that the Croatian police had?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view was that they were really stretched, if I can put it like that, yes, always -- quickly, always the lobby of the police station full of many people with a lot of frustrations and we did not see many Croatian police vehicles on the roads. At least I didn't in my [indiscernible] field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions regarding your statement of February of 2007. That's P677. And if we could go to page 10 of that statement. At the top of that paragraph or at the top of the page you discuss what you observed might be a sweep team because "we had previously seen similar activity in visits to remote villages in the weeks previously. One example being during a visit to a remote village close to the bottom of the Dinara mountain not far from the border of BiH," meaning Bosnia-Herzegovina, "the name of the village, I do recall at the moment." I think you say do not recall, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It should be do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Was there a group of some 15 to 20 Croatian special forces suddenly arrived in an assortment of vehicles and behaved very abruptly to the inhabitants of that village." At least from your experience there, there was nothing about their behaviour that was physically injurious to any of the residents, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nothing of the kind of serious physical assault that we observed while the UN team were there. It was a pretty tense situation, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was a situation in which several ARSK soldiers had been given maps in a way to escape to Bosnia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occasion was in a style of A, B, C. We had gone to the village like on a return visit after being informed of problems from ECMM patrol team, we went there. There was obviously from our presence something wrong, people were very nervous, and then they revealed to us that I think there were one or two men actually in a -- the back of a room in one of the rooms of the villagers. As I recall, there were a few men, they were very afraid, and they did not know what to do. My recall quickly is that they were trying or wanted to get across to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't recall exact flow of the conversation but in the course I think of the next half-hour this group of Croatian special forces arrived by surprise at the village and there was a stand-off and eventually as far as I can recall they were agreement to be handed over to them and the UN would monitor. That's the kind of basic recall I have of everything on that, and I think this is documented in an account by civil affairs and the way that the UN followed up on monitoring it in liaison with the Croatian authorities is documented all through, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, wasn't this a case in which the UN military observers, including you, went to this place on more than one occasion in which some 15 to 20 ARSK soldiers were given maps in a way to try to get to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So if Mr. Tchernetsky testified that as a UN military observer he gave these people maps to try to get to Bosnia and that you were involved in that, you would deny that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would absolutely deny it. The first time I was at this hamlet was on this particular day with my civil affairs and UNHCR colleagues. That's the very, very first time and the only time I was ever there. I absolutely would deny anything like that completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's your position that you were unfailingly neutral throughout this whole process?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My position, I was very objective throughout the whole process, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to make perfectly clear that from your perspective you deny having assisted a group of eight to nine ARSK soldiers, giving them maps in an attempt to evade capture by the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, completely would say I never ever had done that. This is the first occasion I have heard of this information, and the portrayal I have given very briefly of our UN presence is what I recall did happen. The first contact we had of problems was as I recall from ECMM who had suggested that UN Civil Affairs and humanitarian affairs go there to assess the problems in this village. We had certainly no knowledge whatsoever of any so-called RSK soldiers hiding there or being in the vicinity until they came out of the room concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you work together with Mr. Tchernetsky? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not work together with Mr. Tchernetsky. I know was from your recall now UNMO, now, but that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him as a senior UNMO, sometimes deputy UNMO of Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you recall the date of when the activity you were involved in, in assisting these people occurred in August? Was it in August?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on recall, this particular encounter I'm not sure whether it was very close to the situation in Grubori or actually after what happened in Grubori. But I know that it was well documented not by me only in this reference here, so the date and the exact location and the name of the village is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to P204, please. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page, this is the statement, by the way, in evidence of Mr. Tchernetsky, who discusses this incident at the end of August fairly close to the Grubori incident. And it discusses the fact that Mr. Tchernetsky met with two soldiers and he spoke to them and did not report to HQ about the soldiers and only reported about civilians. Now you had said earlier that you had initially met with two soldiers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were men who came out -- when I say me, the UN team who was there, met with or were introduced to these two men. As far as I recall, they were not dressed in a full military uniform. It was a combination, I think, of clothes and, as I recall, some military and that was an issue of concern about what would happen if they were in military uniform. May I just if I could just to read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this before. I think this is something that needs to just be carefully looked at in terms of your raising questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Feel free to read it, and I would suggest you read this portion that ends at the full first paragraph where it says "...detained at Knin school" and then let us know when you are done reading it.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I've pretty much skimmed it as carefully as I can, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Having read that, Mr. Roberts, does that jog your memory at all as to whether or not you were involved in this particular action?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly not involved in any kind of assistance. I was present at the time when the Croatian unit entered the village, and there was a good deal of negotiations done of the special unit colonel was, I would say, firm, polite, in charge, make clear what his responsibilities were, the UN, likewise, said they had an issue of concern of what might happen next and there was a discussion, conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you were present but you were just not involved in bringing them maps?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I certainly was not involved in bringing anybody any maps any time at all. That's not the function of a public affairs or a civil affairs officer. They -- the initial reason for the meeting was as I told you we had gone to the village having been notified as far as I thought by an ECMM team member and were at the village ourselves when all of these things happened, the entry of the special Croatian unit just a short time after, as I recall it, two men had entered from a back room wanting to know from my recall what they should really do. Discussion of maps going into Bosnia-Herzegovina is not anything we were discussing or suggesting from the UN side at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a notation here that said in the -- toward the bottom third of the paragraph: "After the conversation the colonel promised that nobody would be harmed." As far as you know, nobody was harmed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I think nobody was physically assaulted in front of us. It was just, as I said before, quite a tense situation. Colonel -- the Colonel Rasko [phoen] was quite insistent but I understand the reasons why or we understood the reasons why and we, not myself but my colleagues, pointed out okay, there was a need for the UN to observe this and there was agreement what should happen, the process of what should happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So I mean he was obviously trying to arrest armed enemy combatants, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his very clear point. These had been or thought to be combatants, they were hiding and this was the purpose of his -- as I understand and recall, this was the purpose of his particular unit and what they were searching for, and the location of the village, which I still am searching for the exact name, was close to the foot of the mountains. It was really a very unusual village not like you would find on the road. It was very isolated along the side of the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the previous stage, Mr. Roberts, in Mr. Tchernetsky' statement, page 4 and we will get that up on the screen for you, the very bottom. It says the area is a small hamlet between Bukvin Stan [phoen] and Musica Stanovi? Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of the names meaning anything to me at this point in time. It's as I've described it. It certainly would be a place that is not exactly very easy to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull up D99, please. If we could get to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And while we're getting to the next page, this is a report from the special police dated August 28th, 1995 regarding, among other things, this specific incident. If we could go to -- thank you. It discusses you there toward the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Just let me read the thing carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "A member of the United Nations, Alun Roberts, UNCRO spokesman for former Sector South, and another three military observers were found in one of the houses in the cited settlement. They were in the company of five enemy soldiers," and they listed the soldiers, if we could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the same date as the arrival of the Croatian company commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll see who signed the report as we scroll down. It says: "The enlisted persons were not immediately detained in the Knin police department due to the presence of Alun Roberts but it will be done tomorrow in the presence of the fundamental police unit of the Knin police department." It says four automatic rifles, one semi-automatic rifle and one hunting rifle were found in a nearby house. This was the first of two days in this particular incident, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall at all being in the presence of military observers and armed ex-combatant troops in any way at all. I'm trying to recall anything to do with my being present with other UN colleagues to try to ensure that the persons who had been taken by the unit of the special police unit of the colonel at the time, I know we made some later intervention on wanting to visit them but that's I think a completely separate issue to what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not these persons were charged with any criminal complaints involving their activities?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can recall, if this is correct, is that they were -- if this is the right process or the right case exactly, after that group of men all handed themselves over and went with the colonel, either that time or -- yes, it would be -- the reference is the same time that afternoon or day, we, UNHCR, especially wanted to go and check on their security and well-being. As I understood it, they retained part of the school centre in the centre of Knin and there was some problem, I was told by UNHCR, in getting access to them, and I don't want to say here that it's completely correct and it may not be that UNHCR felt that they were still in a big situation of some fear some days after having been taken captive or being arrested. And what happened after in detail, I don't know in terms of the process or the allegations or the -- any kind of trial for -- for military activity that may have been brought against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it typical for a UN press officer to be involved in activity such as this?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying now that the UN press officer was not involved in this. There was a -- it was very regular [Realtime transcript read in error "irregular"] that I go out with human rights action teams to these villages and record them. This is what happened on that day and the rest of this, I don't know who has written it, but in terms of my involvement as portrayed is completely absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness said it was very regular or irregular to go out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very regular for the public information office to accompany HRATs teams. We were in fact part of the HRAT process and we'd go also with UN CIVPOL and UNMOs as they were our UN colleagues on occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's corrected then for the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, you've given I think you said six statements in this case and there were at least one supplemental statement and there are many, many documents that have been tendered through you. There is not one single mention in any statement or in any document that I have seen, and can you correct me if I'm wrong, that mentions General Mladen Markac anywhere does it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's completely correct. I had no conduct as a press officer with General Markac and I had made as far as I can recall no reference to our, the public information office observations of special police or his department or his behaviour. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your two hours also are reduced to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My colleagues are setting a bad precedent, Your Honour. I feel pressure now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have got now two Defence counsel who managed to get two hours and 65 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, we saw the statistics yesterday, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Roberts, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina and he will cross-examine you for 65 minutes. No, no, no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start off with a topic that is dear to the Chamber's hearts, and that is a little background information. First I'd like to talk about generally what the role of a public information office is in a peacekeeping operation and for that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could have the registrar please call up 1D41-0330, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd ask you to ignore the yellow highlights. This is the way I obtained the document. It is irrelevant for purposes of this discussion. This is an excerpt from the handbook on multi-dimensional peacekeeping provided by the United Nations. This is the section on public information in United Nations operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please. If we could go to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Section 1 says: "Priority number one is to communicate," and then the indented paragraph says, "the PIO must explain the presence of the UN mission to the local and international public, the mandate, what the UN mission will do, and what it will not do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Under -- there's the paragraph each commission component. If you could see that.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second paragraph, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The third indented says -- sorry. The first indented says a fully operational public information component brings immediate benefits to the overall mission, bullet point 1, by establishing the UN presence and "showing the flag" in the mission area and internationally. And bullet point 3, by promoting through understanding of the mission mandate and realistic expectations. Says delays in implementing public information activities can give rise to unrealistic expectations and demands sowing the seeds of future disappointment or anger. And then immediately below that, the six objectives of public information, the second paragraph starts, a structured public information office spokesperson, radio, TV video, publications, web site, community outreach has six objectives. Bullet point 1 says, to ensure that the mission's mandate and responsibilities are fully and widely understood. And bullet point 3, to implement a communication strategy that actively supports all the mission's key tasks. Now if we could stop there. I understand that a PIO has a wide variety of responsibilities but would you agree with me that one of the chief functions of a PIO is to explain what the mandate of the UN operation in the theatre is and explain that to the population at large?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpretation and to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that's a general reflection that is accurate, yes. I would also just add that in a conflict situation extra sensitivity needs to be exercised in the ways that those descriptions are put over in close cooperation with political civil affairs officers in the mission area and in the sector areas of any UN international mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page 7 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Talks about within the mission, and actually that yellow highlighted area. You talked about this throughout your now one and a half days of testimony about all information you would receive from the various UN entities in the field. But it says: "The military component (contingents and/or military observers) headed by a Force Commander or chief military observer should regularly update the PIO on its activities." Then it goes on: "Close working relations between the PIO and the military spokesperson or military press liaison officer are indispensable."

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I make just one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. So within the mission the PIO has access to information from various different UN entities in order for you to be able to do your job. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we should be getting support from, from the various departmental heads as well as battalion information sections and UNMOs. Yes, I would just say at the sector level, sector level basis, it is not always that we have a military spokesperson or military press liaison officer of the UN present. That's certainly the case at headquarters level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Talks about PIO local staff, "local staff who are thorough knowledgeable of the society, culture, language and history of the mission area are essential to the success of public information operations." Do you agree with that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also where it continues "they should be viewed as partners rather than merely UN employees," yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify for us who some of your key local staff was in helping you achieve your mission?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. You want me to name them by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that appropriate for the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had -- just very quickly we had a combination office in Knin which was local staff who was a pooled, interpretation pool of about five or six people, and they would serve both the political affairs office and also the civil affairs office in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what their names?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask if it is possible to have this, for various reasons, in closed session, if that is possible. I will explain my reasons for saying that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could go to the next page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The local population, bullet point 3 says: "All mission personnel must remain non-partisan and objective in their behaviour. Public information personnel in particular must be conscious of maintaining impartiality in their conversation and private statements. Sympathy to a cause or a party must not be permitted to undermine the mission's credibility and affect the PIO's outputs or the behaviour of its staff. Impartiality however should be not be confused with neutrality. UN staff are expected to be impartial at all times but not neutral in the face of, for example, human rights violations." Mr. Roberts, did you at all times while you were working as the PIO in Sector South -- I should say did you and your staff at all times maintain the impartiality as described in this portion of the UN handbook on multi-dimensional peacekeeping?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the promotion of the work I felt that we were impartial in the work that we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I note you said in the promotion of the work. Were there times when you were not impartial outside of times where you were promoting your work?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were at all times impartial, but in terms especially of the contact with journalists and the contact with media agencies that was promoting the objectives and mandates, I think that was very important we were impartial in the way that that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, is that an answer to the question? The question was whether outside the area you mentioned whether you were impartial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Impartial at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Impartial at all times, all activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that goes for your staff as well, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've talked about -- we've seen what the handbook says about the PIO working to explain the mandate to the public at large and we note from your statements that you arrived in the theatre in Sector South in August of 1993. So if we could first take a look at --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Middle September, but it is not a big issue. Middle of September 1995 is when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, if I could tender the document on the screen into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, apparently. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit D696.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D696 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have 1D41-0290.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a few documents just to save time, Mr. Roberts, but this is no -- you said you arrived in mid-September 1993. This is it resolution 871 of the Security Council which was passed a few weeks after you arrived in the theatre as the PIO. You will note on the first page towards the middle, the Security Council: "Deeply concerned that the United Nations peacekeeping plan for the Republic of Croatia and all relevant Security Council resolutions, in particular Resolution 769, have not yet been fully implemented," and I'll show you the resolution in a moment, but while this is on the screen, if we could turn to the next page. Paragraph 3: "Security Council condemns once again continuing military attacks within the territory of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and reaffirms its commitment to ensure respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now, Madam Registrar, if we could call up the peacekeeping plan which was referenced on the first page, which is 1D41-0268. If we go to page 15, please. This is it annex 3 referred to in that Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, do you intend to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tender Resolution 87? Let's try to keep the list as short as possible. I take it no objections. Madam Registrar, that would be 1D41-0290 which recently was on our screen. That would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be exhibit D697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D697 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is the annex referred in the 1993 Security Council resolution. It's the concept for United Nations peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia. If we could go to the next page, please. The basic concept, paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The United Nations troops and police monitors would be deployed in certain areas in Croatia designated as United Nations protected areas. These areas would be demilitarized. All armed forces in them would be either withdrawn or disbanded. The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the areas remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack. The role of the United Nations police monitors would be to ensure that the local police forces carried out their duties without discriminating against persons of any nationality or abusing anyone's human rights." The last sentence says: "The United Nations force would also, as appropriate, assist the humanitarian agencies of the United Nations in the return of all displaced persons who so desired to their homes in the UNPAs." If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just go back to that page you were on? Just one moment, if I could?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Just would quickly for the information we're focussing on in terms of this document as part of the history of the UN presence, paragraph eight, first sentence: "The UNPAs would be areas in Croatia in which the Secretary-General judged that special arrangements were required during interim period to ensure that a lasting cease-fire was maintained." And in the document you had earlier, sir, paragraph 6 of it talks about the need for a lasting cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, perhaps apparently you consider certain aspects of special importance or special relevance. If at the end of your testimony you would think that we really missed something important, then you can add it, but please first wait for Mr. Misetic to put his questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please. Towards the bottom, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The function of protecting the inhabitants of the UNPAs would be shared between the United Nations forces infantry units and its civilian police monitors. The infantry would ensure that the UNPAs remained demilitarised. The police monitors would ensure the local police carried out their duties without discrimination against any nationality and with full respect for the human rights of all residents of the UNPAs." Paragraph 11 towards the middle: "They would also investigate any complaints made to them about violations of the demilitarised status of the UNPAs, any confirmed violations would be taken up with the offending party and would, if necessary, be reported by the Secretary-General to the Security Council." And if we could go to paragraph 20, just -- not paragraph 20, page 20. This section is entitled return of displaced persons to their homes. "In accordance with the established international principles, the United Nations policy is to facilitate the return to their homes of all persons displaced by the recent hostilities who so desire. The lead in this matter is being taken by the humanitarian agencies of the United Nations. If a United Nations force were established in Yugoslavia, it would provide all appropriate support to this effort in the UNPAs. The United Nations police monitors would have an especially important role in this regard." Now, Mr. Roberts, we have seen a Security Council resolution passed three weeks after your arrival, and let me just ask you, as the PIO, were you regularly working with the local Serb population and leadership and emphasizing the fact that United Nations resolutions and the peacekeeping plan called on the Serbs to demilitarise, called on all attacks against non-Serbs in the UNPAs and violations of human rights to cease and that all persons who had been previously displaced should be allowed to return to their homes? Was that part of your public information campaign?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just go from when I arrived in the mission on the way down to Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you between September of 1993 and August 4 1995, were you engaged in those activities to have -- to explain the mandate as passed by the Security Council to the local Serb population and its leaders?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in explaining that in partnership with my political colleagues under the direction, I have to say, of our SRSG and our chief of public information in Zagreb. On the way down to Knin to be the spokesperson, I was well briefed on the evening I went, what to expect, what to try and do, and that's basically why I was being brought from Skopje to be in Sector South Knin. It was labelled to be a strong proactive public information presence in Sector South and throughout the sector, linking up with my colleague in the Sector North public information office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, would you agree with me -- or I should better say, the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal in the Martic case at paragraph 299 made a finding that "there is considerable evidence that Croats were being displaced until the end of 1994." And I also have reports of the Special Rapporteur Mr. Mazowiecki from 1994 talking about continuing human rights abuses of the remaining Croat population in these areas.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have for you so that can you take look at the break every comment attributed to you in the English speaking world press, I should say, from September 1993 to 4 August 1995. There's 62 articles, and I will put it to you and allow you to review it during the break, that not one time did you make a comment calling attention to the fact that the human rights of Croats in the area were being abused. Would you agree with that you?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not. You're saying English speaking press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, my role was to talk to the public opinion and the policy makers in Knin and the so-called Krajina, and the very first press briefings I was permitted to have through headquarters, I made an oversight of what our humanitarian affairs office of the UN had observed and documented in much the same way as you have said here, and the basic response was that the press would not take that information and report it. The day after we saw nothing covered in the Knin media at all in terms of the way that I had stated to the media at a public information conference that kind of representation of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask my question again. Do you agree with me that in the English speaking press for those almost two years, do you agree that you never made a comment in the international press, English speaking, calling attention to the ongoing human rights abuses against the non-Serb population in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with you. I can't remember why it's not there, but I know on certainly more than four, five occasions interviews with international journalists where I pointed these observations out at the beginning of the UNPA by UN personnel who were deployed and those accounts were well documented and I had them to pass on and I did pass them on on more than one occasion, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will hand the binders and let you to take a look on the break to see which journalists you may have spoken to that didn't publish it. I will also call your attention to the fact that of the 62 articles, 31 of them deal with HV troop movements. One is for the witness, Madam Usher, and one is for the Prosecution. If the Trial Chamber wishes to have copies, I have for the Trial Chamber as well. But I also note if you could explain to me then, I have a second binder if you wish from 4 August 1995 to 31 December 1995 -- I'm sorry. Both are -- both sections are in your binder. Where you make extensive comments in the international English speaking press about human rights abuses in Sector South, and I'm wondering if you could explain to us why after Operation Storm, you were on a very regular basis in the international press about human rights violations, but for the almost two years prior to that, at least I can't find a single reference. Can you explain why that might be?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly explain that in the two years previously we were doing a lot in Sector South to try and get international press attention in to the Sector South area directly, to travel widely and report, and we did not get, I think, the focus that I wanted the international press to come in to Sector South to conduct interviews, to hear the views of UN personnel besides myself who would make those kinds of observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So your testimony is you were trying to do it, it was just that the international press wasn't interested in the human rights abuses? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were, but the issue I would draw to your attention, sir, is the great difficulty we with the Serbs in Knin to permit international journalists to travel into the UNPAs through Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, would that mean that the Croatians afterwards were providing that kind of access to allow international journalists to report on human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time that I was the press officer we had this rebel regime of the Krajina Serbs and they held that territory. You couldn't go in there without any special paper being provided. When the Krajina had fallen and the Republic of Croatia had taken back the whole territory, journalists came in. There was no opposition for them to not be able to travel in and down from Zagreb very easily and quickly. It was certainly a problem of getting any international press in. You had two options, which was, one, to come across from Belgrade through the corridor again held by Bosnian Serb forces, and two is to come in through Zagreb through some special consent from the United Nations press office in Zagreb, or you had phone call communication with those journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, we've seen your own list of how many international correspondents went through your own office, correct? They didn't have any particular problem from the Croatian government getting into the theatre and being able to report?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is after the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Obviously, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a big difference, an extremely big difference between the situation in the war conflict area that I was dealing with in the course of mid-September, 1993 until the 4th of August when we had one complete country and people can come in from Zagreb and come down by road as they did, but that was the not case before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is that there was -- you noticed yourself a difference between how much access was being granted by Croatian authorities after Storm and how much access to international journalists was being given by the Krajina Serb authorities prior to Operation Storm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very good difference for the simple reason the territory was not completely one in the hands of the Croatian government in Zagreb. Beforehand, we didn't have that situation, which is the obvious reason of much of this documentation by the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I tender this document into evidence please and we can take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it then that this is a separate document. You said earlier that it was attached to the other one. It is not yet part of it because it has a different -- it's the one on our screen at this moment. It's 1D41-0268. You earlier said that this was attached or related at least in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's only referenced in the 1993 Security Council resolution from 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is a separate document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- being a UN document, I do not expect any objections. In the absence of objections, Madam Registrar, this would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit D698, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D698 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- while he's looking at the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say then that the Krajina Serb authorities were allowing to you comment internationally or giving you enough access so that you could internationally comment on HV troop movements, but on human rights issues that you were having a problem reporting on that? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't I don't think so. I think that I reported to a number of international press on human rights problems. I remember reporting about the several villages of Croats inside the sector, inside the UNPA in terms of various threats and abuse that they were receiving. Pod Lapac was one near Korenica, which was a special UN concern, and we explained to the Serb journalists and Serb politicians very clearly that when we got towards the late part of 1994 the purpose of UNPA and UNPROFOR was not to protect the so-called Serb community of the UNPAs. It had been originally to protect the inhabitants inside the rebellion areas of Croatia, including especially the Croat population in the UNPAs, and I did report on those --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who did you complain to?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To complain to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you complain to the international press about this problem with the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of the fact of getting any negotiations going in terms of their responsibilities and impartiality was almost a loggerhead to get that kind of negotiation going and we made that public both locally and to a number of international journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you name the journalists?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I name the -- Misha Glenny was one. John Pomfret, Washington Post, was another one. Certainly, interviews from CNN, another one. There were several serious stand-offs between the Croat military and the Serbs and we responded in terms of what we were doing especially in regard to the Croat minority population to ensure that they stayed, but it was very tense. And that, I think, was to New York Times, Chris Hedges. Certainly there was Owen Stuart Bennett -- or Bennett-Jones, BBC World Service Radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's -- in order to get to the break, you have your binder in front of you. If you can look through that and see whether there's any such articles. There's an index at the beginning for you and if you could tab for us during the break where those appear, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we may need more a little bit more than the break it's the first time I've seen this, but I can try to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's give it a first attempt now and if you need more time, then there might be another break later today, Mr. Roberts. Could you also -- because I'd like to put a question to you, perhaps you could consider it already without answering it now. You said that there was quite a difference between getting access to the Krajina, driving down the road from Zagreb when the Croats had -- were in control compared to the previous situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Serb were in control. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was easier to drive down the road to Krajina once the Croats had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Taken control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether an issue that came up as far as the UN agencies are concerned whether the freedom of movement of the journalists in the area was also secured or whether they were just having access to Knin and the roads or whether there had a possibility to travel around and to observe what happened. I'm not asking you to give an answer now, because we will have a break first. And we resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start, but, as I said sometime, sometimes the breaks are more busy than we are here in Court where you are keeping the right pace. Mr. Misetic, you're invited to continue the right pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, were you able to find the articles by the reporters you referenced in the binder during the break?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through the binder. I thought I was supposed to mark the articles where I was not quoted properly in terms of being objective. I didn't find articles of those that you referred to, no. But I would like the opportunity to try and find those articles myself. I don't see them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me say I don't think I said find articles where you're not being objective. I said find articles where you are being quoted concerning human rights abuses against Croats prior to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Or non-Serbs, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, in this file that you have compiled and have given me to look at now, first, for the record it's the first time that I have seen this document, obviously. I do not see in this compilation in the first maybe ten, 12 articles I looked at myself responding or talking about or being interviewed specifically by the journalists on the issue of human rights issues in Croatia. What we have here on the first small number over a -- I think 100 or so selections that you have put together very neatly, I got as far as only the first 12 and hopped on then to number 30. These are journalists and articles that concern the initial cease-fire agreement of March 1994 and its implementation and the role of the United Nations and observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- to be fair to you, I'm going to be continuing into the morning. We'll let you take that binder with you tonight back to the hotel and you can look at it. Let me just tell you, the selection criteria that we used was putting the name Alun Roberts, spelling it both Alun with U and Alan with an A in case there was typo, putting it into the database and running every article that mentions your name from August 1993, actually, until 4 August 1995 and then in the tab in the back is from 4 August 1995 to 31 December 1995. So when you go back what I'm telling you is those are the articles that mention your name, go back and see whether you are quoted anywhere as bringing human rights abuses to the attention of the international public.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no problem with that at all. May I also at the time of coming back give with a response to that give a fair observation of what these interviews and articles of the journalists focus on section by section? I have no problem with the first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me actually follow up with that, because I wanted to follow up with that right now. Mr. Kuzmanovic asked you about your archive that you maintain. In that archive do you have pictures taken by your UN camera of the human rights abuses that were taking place against Croats from the time you arrived in Sector South until 4 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't in the archive but I did pass on some photographs to head office in Zagreb I think late 1994, maybe even 1993 also. This was a visit of the then head of civil affairs, Cedric Thornberry whose name I think you maybe are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the very first deputy head of mission when I arrived from Skopje into the Sector South area and he brought me or ordered me to be transferred to be in Sector South Knin. There were two meetings I think in Pod Lapac where there was concern about the stability and the safety of the Croats. There was no violence against them but we took photographs of the situation but we had no conflict zone at that time against the village. I can say I produced to headquarters office photographs of broken Croat villages, hamlets, some near Drnis, some near the way out towards Benkovac and some around the area of I think up towards Korenica and beyond that were destroyed. I didn't know they were broken Croat villages but we were told by people who knew that this was the situation prior to and during the whole rebellion establishment of the Serb Krajina forces in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me pause for a minute. We've seen admitted into evidence a list maintained by you and Judy Jacob regarding the number of bodies in Sector South. Do you also have a list of people killed in Sector South from the time you arrived as the PIO until 4 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there a reason that you didn't keep such a list prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly because there was no big conflict or war conflict that was taking place. There were reports that I would follow by UNHCR of problems inside Sector South with the Croats but I did not document specific instances of the villages concerned and so on, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --
